faq.a: Chlorophyll is the green pigment in chloroplasts. It absorbs light energy, mostly red and blue, and passes it on to make sugar in photosynthesis.

faq.q: Why don't plants use green light?
faq.a: They do use some, especially deep inside the leaf, but chlorophyll absorbs green much less than red and blue. Scientists think this may protect plants from taking in too much energy in bright, changing sunlight.
Yes. Plants with red or purple leaves, like the copper beech, still contain chlorophyll. Red pigments called anthocyanins cover up the green.

faq.q: Are there plants that are not green?
faq.a: A few plants have no chlorophyll at all, like the ghost plant and dodder. They cannot make food, so they take it from fungi or from other plants.
asks: Can a plant live without chlorophyll?

faq.q: Why are some seaweeds red or brown?
faq.a: Seaweeds living deeper underwater have extra pigments that catch the blue-green light that reaches them, which makes them look red or brown. They still have chlorophyll too.
asks: Why is seaweed not always green?

facts: Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue light and absorbs much less green.
Copper beech trees have purple leaves because anthocyanin pigments mask their chlorophyll.
Dodder has little or no chlorophyll and lives as a parasite on other plants.
